Install Codon's JIT with pip: pip install codon-jit Save the following code to file primes.py: import codon from time import time def is_prime_python(n): if n <= 1: return False for i in range(2, n): if n % i == 0: return False return True @codon.jit def is_prime_codon(n): if n <= 1: return False for i in range(2, n): if n % i == 0: return False return True t0 = time() ans = sum(1 for i in range(100000, 200000) if is_prime_python(i)) t1 = time() print(f'[python] {ans} | took {t1 - t0} seconds') t0 = time() ans = sum(1 for i in range(100000, 200000) if is_prime_codon(i)) t1 = time() print(f'[codon] {ans} | took {t1 - t0} seconds') Run with Python: python3 primes.py

Markdown Classes group state and behavior using Python's familiar syntax. A regular class creates reference objects, so several names can refer to the same instance. For example, this class stores a point's coordinates and provides a readable string representation: class Point: def __init__(self, x, y): self.x = x self.y = y def __str__(self): return f'({self.x}, {self.y})' p = Point(3, 4) print(p) # (3, 4) Codon will automatically infer class fields if none are specified explicitly. Alternatively, the class fields can be specified in the class body: class Point: x: int y: int def __init__(self, x, y): self.x = x self.y = y def __str__(self): return f'({self.x}, {self.y})' Class fields can reference the enclosing class through the Optional type: class Point: x: int y: int other: Optional[Point] def __init__(self, x, y, other: Optional[Point] = None): self.x = x self.y = y self.other = other def __str__(self): if self.other is None: return f'({self.x}, {self.y})' else: return f'({self.x}, {self.y}) -> {str(self.other)}' p = Point(3, 4) print(p) # (3, 4) q = Point(5, 6, p) print(q) # (5, 6) -> (3, 4)

Codon reports a compile-time error when a field may be uninitialized when __init__ returns normally. The check follows calls to known helper functions and methods, including base constructors called through super(). Initialization can therefore be split across helpers: class Buffer: values: list[int] def __init__(self): self.initialize() def initialize(self): self.values = [] The analysis is conservative: assignments on only one branch do not guarantee initialization, and initialization that cannot be verified statically may still produce an error. The check applies to regular classes; tuple classes and compiler-internal classes are exempt. Tuple classes return complete tuple values from __new__ rather than initializing fields through __init__. The check verifies initialization rather than supplying default values or adding runtime guards. A field therefore needs a value before code reads it, even when its initialization is delegated to a helper.

Reference classes can define a static __new__ method to control allocation or return an existing instance. Constructor arguments are evaluated once and passed to both the custom __new__ and __init__. If __new__ returns an unrelated type, __init__ is skipped. Most classes only need __init__; custom allocation is useful when the ordinary creation of a new instance is not the desired behavior.

A property exposes a computed value through attribute syntax. A setter can translate an assignment back into the object's stored representation, keeping the conversion in one place: class Temperature: celsius: float def __init__(self, celsius: float): self.celsius = celsius @property def fahrenheit(self) -> float: return self.celsius * 9.0 / 5.0 + 32.0 @fahrenheit.setter def fahrenheit(self, value: float): self.celsius = (value - 32.0) * 5.0 / 9.0 temperature = Temperature(100.0) print(temperature.fahrenheit) # 212.0 temperature.fahrenheit = 32.0 print(temperature.celsius) # 0.0 An ordinary field belongs to each instance, whereas a ClassVar belongs to the class. For example, a shared counter can assign identifiers as objects are created: class Record: next_identifier: ClassVar[int] = 0 identifier: int def __init__(self): self.identifier = Record.next_identifier Record.next_identifier += 1 first = Record() second = Record() print(first.identifier, second.identifier) # 0 1 Here, each record keeps its own identifier while creation updates a common counter. As with other shared mutable state, concurrent updates require appropriate synchronization.

An unannotated instance-method argument named self has type Self. Codon binds Self to the receiver's static type, so an inherited method can use the derived type without upcasting to the class that defined the method: class A: def foo(self): return f"{type(self)} ({Self})" class B(A): pass print(A().foo()) # <class 'A'> (<class 'A'>) print(B().foo()) # <class 'B'> (<class 'B'>) Return types are inferred normally. A method can also explicitly annotate its return type as Self if needed. An explicit self annotation such as self: Context keeps that annotation and does not default to Self. Self also works for tuple classes and can be declared explicitly as a generic parameter (Self: type), including in static methods. It does not itself make a method virtual.

In Python, class methods can be defined to take arguments of arbitrary types, and to reason about them through functions like isinstance(). While the same works in Codon, Codon also offers another way to separate out method logic for different input types: method overloading. Multiple methods with the same name but different arguments or argument types can be defined in the same class. Codon will use the method corresponding to the argument types provided in a given call of that method. For example: class Point: def __init__(self, x: int, y: int): self.x = x self.y = y def distance(self, other: Point): return abs(self.x - other.x) + abs(self.y - other.y) def distance(self, x: int, y: int): return self.distance(Point(x, y)) p = Point(3, 4) print(p.distance(Point(0, 0))) # 7 print(p.distance(2, 2)) # 3 Both overloads calculate Manhattan distance. One accepts another point, while the other accepts coordinates and delegates to the first implementation. Method resolution occurs bottom-up, meaning that if multiple methods are applicable to a call, the latest definition is selected. note Non-method functions can also be overloaded in Codon by adding the @overload decorator, which prevents later definitions from shadowing previous ones. See function overloading for an example.

Regular classes are mutable and passed around by reference. Internally, class data is dynamically allocated and a pointer to the allocated data is used to represent the class instance. Codon also supports tuple classes, whose fields form a value that can be stored inline rather than requiring a separately allocated object. Their fields cannot be reassigned after construction, making them useful for small records such as coordinates or measurements. The @tuple annotation selects this representation: @tuple class Point: x: int y: int def __str__(self): return f'({self.x}, {self.y})' Because tuple class instances are immutable, tuple classes do not use the usual __init__ method, and can instead define new constructors via the __new__ method. A default __new__ which takes all of the tuple class's fields as arguments is automatically generated. We can define additional __new__ methods as follows, for instance: @tuple class Point: x: int y: int # constructor (A) def __new__(): return Point(0, 0) # constructor (B) def __new__(x: int): return Point(x, 0) def __str__(self): return f'({self.x}, {self.y})' zero = Point() # calls constructor (A) one = Point(1) # calls constructor (B) print(zero) # (0, 0) print(one) # (1, 0) Assigning zero.x = 1 would be a compilation error because tuple fields are immutable. This restriction applies to the fields themselves: a list stored in a tuple field is still a mutable list, and copying the tuple does not deep-copy such referenced objects. Tuple classes can be more efficient than reference classes when many small records are stored in an array or list. They do not participate in class inheritance, either as subclasses or as base classes. Composition, such as storing a Point in a field of another record, lets a larger value reuse its data and methods without an inheritance relationship. Internally, tuple classes correspond to C structs. For example, the Point tuple class above would correspond exactly to the following struct definition in C: struct Point { int64_t x; int64_t y; }; As a result, tuple classes can also be used when interoperating with a C API, as they can mirror API-specific data structures or layouts.

Codon supports Python's inheritance and dynamic polymorphism. For example: class Shape: def area(self): return 0.0 def describe(self): return "This is a shape." class Circle(Shape): radius: float def __init__(self, radius): self.radius = radius def area(self): return 3.1416 * self.radius**2 def describe(self): return f"A circle with radius {self.radius}" class Rectangle(Shape): width: float height: float def __init__(self, width, height): self.width = width self.height = height def area(self): return self.width * self.height def describe(self): return f"A rectangle with width {self.width} and height {self.height}" class Square(Rectangle): def __init__(self, width): super().__init__(width, width) def describe(self): return super().describe().replace('rectangle', 'square') shapes: list[Shape] = [] shapes.append(Circle(5)) shapes.append(Rectangle(4, 6)) shapes.append(Square(3)) for shape in shapes: print(shape.describe(), f'(area={shape.area()})') The annotation list[Shape] gives the collection a common element type while allowing it to hold instances of different subclasses. Calls to area() and describe() through that common type select the implementation for the actual object: Circle and Rectangle override both methods, while Square inherits Rectangle.area() and supplies its own describe(). super() lets a subclass reuse the next implementation in Python's method resolution order. Here, Square.__init__() delegates field initialization to Rectangle.__init__(), and Square.describe() adapts the description returned by its parent. This is useful when a subclass changes one part of a behavior without duplicating the rest of its implementation. For a collection such as this one, the base class describes the interface that all elements share. Members introduced only by a particular subclass, such as Circle.radius, are not part of that shared interface; an isinstance() check can narrow an element to the subclass before accessing them: for shape in shapes: if isinstance(shape, Circle): print(shape.radius) # 5.0

Use Enum to define named singleton values: from enum import Enum, auto class Color(Enum): RED = auto() GREEN = auto() BLUE = auto() CRIMSON = RED assert Color.RED.name == 'RED' assert Color.RED.value == 1 assert Color(1) is Color.RED assert Color['CRIMSON'] is Color.RED assert list(Color) == [Color.RED, Color.GREEN, Color.BLUE] Equal values become aliases of the first member. Iteration skips aliases and preserves declaration order; Color.__members__ includes all declared names. Members support identity comparisons, equality, hashing, and use as dictionary keys. Enum subclasses may define methods and be nested inside other classes. Class iteration, subscription, length, and containment use ordinary static methods inherited from Enum, and __members__ is a normal ClassVar. These follow Codon's usual attribute lookup and override rules. Calling an enum with an unknown value raises ValueError; an unknown member name raises KeyError. Existing members cannot be reassigned, and an enum with members cannot be subclassed to add more members. Codon supports class-based Enum declarations with one native value type per enumeration, including integer and string values. auto() generates integer values starting at 1, or one above the largest preceding value. Custom __init__/__new__ constructors, enum mixins, the functional Enum(...) factory, IntEnum, and flag types are not currently supported.

Markdown Codon distinguishes errors discovered while compiling from exceptions raised by a running program. An unsupported operation between known types is a compilation error; invalid input, missing files and similar conditions can instead be handled with Python's exception syntax. This distinction is useful when diagnosing a failure: a try block can handle an exception from native code, but cannot make a program with a type-checking error compile.

An exception can communicate why a value cannot be used, leaving the caller to decide how to report or recover from the problem: def parse_count(text: str) -> int: count = int(text) if count < 0: raise ValueError("count must be nonnegative") return count try: count = parse_count("-3") except ValueError as error: print(f"Invalid count: {error}") else: print(f"Count: {count}") # Invalid count: count must be nonnegative The handler covers both a failed integer conversion and the explicit nonnegative check. The else block runs when the protected operation succeeds, which keeps successful processing separate from error reporting. Catching the exception type expected at this boundary also allows unrelated failures to reach their own callers instead of being hidden. Within a handler, a bare raise propagates the current exception again. This can be useful when a layer adds logging but leaves recovery to a higher-level caller. If an absent result is an ordinary outcome rather than an error, Optional is another way to express it.

A with statement keeps a resource's lifetime together with the code that uses it. For example, suppose counts.txt contains: counts.txt 2 3 5 The following function reads and sums its nonblank lines: def sum_file(filename: str) -> int: total = 0 with open(filename, encoding="utf-8") as stream: for line in stream: text = line.strip() if text: total += int(text) return total print(sum_file("counts.txt")) # 10 The stream closes when control leaves the with block, including when a conversion raises an exception or the function returns early. Reading the file line by line also avoids constructing a list containing the entire file. If decoding fails or a line is not an integer, the exception remains available to the caller; closing the file does not turn that failure into a successful result. Specifying an encoding makes the text format explicit. Binary files use a mode such as "rb" and return bytes rather than str, without performing a text-decoding step. Native pathlib also provides path objects and filesystem operations when an application needs more than a file name. For cleanup that is not represented by a context manager, a finally block runs as control leaves its associated try statement, whether processing succeeds, raises or returns. Keeping cleanup in with or finally avoids having to repeat it across each exit path.

Debug mode retains source information and disables optimizations, making it a useful starting point for investigating a failure: codon run -debug program.py Normal exception handling remains available in release builds as well. The separate -disable-exceptions option removes that mechanism: raising an exception traps rather than transferring control to a handler. Programs that depend on input validation or recovery should retain exception handling; the compiler options describe the relevant settings.

Markdown Functions in Codon use Python's def syntax, with positional arguments, keyword arguments and default values. Their bodies are compiled for the types used by the program; annotations can describe an interface, while unannotated parameters allow the compiler to infer the appropriate specializations.

This function scales a list of measurements. Its annotations describe the input and output element types, while the default factor keeps the common case convenient: def scale(values: list[float], factor: float = 2.0) -> list[float]: return [value * factor for value in values] print(scale([1.0, 2.5])) # [2.0, 5.0] print(scale([1.0, 2.5], factor=3.0)) # [3.0, 7.5] Removing the annotations would allow the same definition to specialize for other suitable input types. The generics guide covers that model and shows how to relate an argument's type to the elements of a collection. A function can return several values as a tuple, which callers can unpack into separate names: def bounds(values): return min(values), max(values) lower, upper = bounds([8, 3, 12]) print(lower, upper) # 3 12 The number of returned tuple fields is fixed, although their values are computed at runtime. A function with no explicit return value produces None; when a meaningful result may be absent, an optional return type can make that possibility explicit.

Functions and lambdas can be passed to other functions, allowing a shared iteration pattern to work with different operations: def transform(values, operation): return [operation(value) for value in values] def magnitude(value: int) -> int: return abs(value) print(transform([-2, 3], magnitude)) # [2, 3] print(transform([-2, 3], lambda value: value * value)) # [4, 9] Here, the compiler specializes transform() for the supplied callable and input collection. Passing an operation explicitly is often useful when the same traversal needs different filtering, formatting or numerical behavior.

An ordinary second definition of a function replaces the first. Adding @overload instead keeps the earlier definition available and lets Codon select an implementation from the arguments' types: def render(value): return str(value) @overload def render(value: float): return f"{value:.2f}" print(render(3.14159)) # 3.14 print(render("ready")) # ready Resolution proceeds from the most recent definition toward earlier ones, using the first applicable overload. Placing a general implementation before more specialized ones therefore provides a fallback without hiding them. Class methods support overloading without requiring the decorator on each definition.

A function containing yield produces a generator. Its body supplies values as the caller requests them, which makes generators useful for processing a sequence without first building another complete list: def nonblank(lines): for line in lines: text = line.strip() if text: yield text records = nonblank([" oak ", "", "pine"]) print(list(records)) # ['oak', 'pine'] print(list(records)) # [] A generator is consumed as it is iterated; constructing a new one is necessary to repeat the traversal. Converting it to a list, as above, materializes the remaining values. A for loop can instead consume them incrementally, and a generator expression offers a compact form for simple transformations: values = [1, 2, 3, 4] total = sum(value * value for value in values if value % 2 == 0) print(total) # 20 When iteration depends on an open file or another resource, that resource needs to remain available until iteration finishes. The exceptions and resources guide shows how a with block can keep file processing and cleanup together.

Markdown Codon infers types from the way values are created and used, which often leaves ordinary Python code free of annotations. Explicit types become useful when describing an interface, choosing the element type of an empty collection, or expressing relationships between a function's inputs and outputs. A generic definition leaves some of those types open until it is used. For example, list[int] and list[str] share a container implementation while storing different element types. A generic function can make the same kind of distinction without requiring a separate source definition for each type.

Container annotations describe the types stored in a collection, not its current contents or length. A type alias can give a frequently used combination a convenient name: Counts = dict[str, int] def add_count(counts: Counts, name: str): counts[name] = counts.get(name, 0) + 1 counts: Counts = {} add_count(counts, "oak") add_count(counts, "oak") print(counts["oak"]) # 2 The dictionary can grow at runtime, while its key and value types remain str and int. Counts is an alias for that dictionary type, rather than a new container class.

Optional[T] represents either a value of type T or None. It is useful for operations that may have no result without treating that outcome as an error: def first_positive(values: list[int]) -> Optional[int]: for value in values: if value > 0: return value return None result = first_positive([-3, 0, 7]) if result is not None: print(result + 1) # 8 else: print("No positive value") Checking for None before using the result makes both cases visible to the reader and allows the non-empty branch to work with the underlying value. For a default argument, the same annotation can distinguish an omitted value from a meaningful value such as zero.

Union describes a finite set of alternatives. This gives a collection a single element type while still allowing its elements to hold different kinds of values: values: list[Union[int, str]] = [2, "ready"] for value in values: if isinstance(value, int): print(value + 1) # 3 else: print(value.upper()) # READY The isinstance() check selects the operation appropriate to the stored value. Unlike the compile-time checks in a function specialized for one concrete type, a union may need this distinction at runtime. When alternatives share a common interface, a base class can be a more useful representation than enumerating each concrete type in a union.

Imagine we want to enforce that a particular function should only accept a list argument; we can achieve that using generic types: def foo[T](x: list[T]): # 'T' is a generic type parameter print(max(x)) foo([20, 42, 12]) # 42 foo(['hello', 'world']) # world info This syntax is supported by Python 3.12 and up. See PEP 695. In this code, T is a generic type parameter that gets realized based on the argument type: foo([20, 42, 12]) → the argument is a list of integers, so T is realized as int. foo(['hello', 'world']) → the argument is a list of strings, so T is realized as str. foo(100) → the argument is not a list at all, so a type checking error occurs. For comparison, the following call is intentionally invalid and fails during compilation, before the program runs: foo(100) Alternatively, Codon allows the generic type parameter to be specified as an argument: def foo(x: list[T], T: type): print(max(x)) foo([20, 42, 12], int) # can specify 'T' explicitly... foo([20, 42, 12], T=int) # ... or by name foo([20, 42, 12]) # still works; 'T' inferred This syntax is useful for allowing generic type parameters to be specified explicitly as arguments when the function is called, or for providing default values for them: def bar(x: list[T], T: type = int): print(type(x)) bar([]) # <class 'List[int]'>

Classes can also be generic: class A[T]: # 'T' is a generic type parameter x: T def __init__(self, x: T): self.x = x def __repr__(self): return f'A({self.x})' x = A(42) # 'T' inferred y = A[str]('hello') # 'T' explicitly given as 'str' print(x) # A(42) print(y) # A(hello) Generic type parameters can also be listed after the class fields: class A: # identical to above definition x: T T: type def __init__(self, x: T): self.x = x

Markdown Codon supports inline LLVM IR via the @llvm annotation: @llvm def llvm_add(a: int, b: int) -> int: %res = add i64 %a, %b ret i64 %res print(llvm_add(3, 4)) # 7 Note that LLVM functions must explicitly specify argument and return types. LLVM functions can also be generic, and a format specifier in the body will be replaced by the appropriate LLVM type: @llvm def llvm_add[T](a: T, b: T) -> T: %res = add {=T} %a, %b ret {=T} %res print(llvm_add(3, 4)) # 7 print(llvm_add(i8(5), i8(6))) # 11 The substitution chooses a type, not an instruction. This example uses the integer add instruction, so a floating-point implementation would need fadd instead. LLVM intrinsics can be accessed with declare: @llvm def popcnt(n: int) -> int: declare i64 @llvm.ctpop.i64(i64) %0 = call i64 @llvm.ctpop.i64(i64 %n) ret i64 %0 print(popcnt(42)) # 3

An inline LLVM function returning Codon's None uses an empty structure as its LLVM return value, rather than ret void. For example, a helper that writes through a pointer can be defined as follows: @llvm def store_value(pointer: Ptr[int], value: int) -> None: store i64 %value, ptr %pointer, align 1 ret {} zeroinitializer buffer = Ptr[int](1) store_value(buffer, 42) print(buffer[0]) # 42 The pointer still needs to refer to writable storage for an integer; inline LLVM does not add bounds or lifetime checks. This function intentionally has no purity annotation because its store changes memory visible to the caller.

Sometimes it can be helpful to annotate @llvm functions to give the compiler more information as to how they behave. Codon has a number of default annotations for LLVM functions (all of which also apply to external/C functions): @pure: Function does not capture arguments (aside from return value capturing as in def foo(x): return x), does not modify arguments, and has no side effects. This is a mathematically "pure" function. @no_side_effect: Very similar to @pure but function may return different results on different calls, such as the C function time(). @nocapture: Function does not capture any of its arguments (again excluding return value capturing). @self_captures: Function's first (self) argument captures the other arguments, an example being List.__setitem__(). These are mutually-exclusive annotations. Another complementary annotation can be used to indicate that the return value of the function captures its arguments: @derives: Return value of the function captures its arguments. These annotations describe contracts that the optimizer may rely on; they do not add runtime checks. Correct annotations preserve the function's intended behavior while enabling optimizations, but an incorrect contract can cause operations to be removed or reordered. When a function's effects are not clear, leaving an annotation out is preferable to making an unsupported promise.
Markdown Codon provides various low-level programming features that can be used in performance-sensitive settings or when interfacing with external APIs.

While Codon's standard int type is a 64-bit signed integer, different integer types are made available through the Int and UInt types: Int[N]: Signed integer with N bits UInt[N]: Unsigned integer with N bits For example: a = Int[16](42) # signed 16-bit integer 42 b = UInt[128](99) # unsigned 128-bit integer 99 The Codon standard library provides shorthands for the common variants: i8/u8: signed/unsigned 8-bit integer i16/u16: signed/unsigned 16-bit integer i32/u32: signed/unsigned 32-bit integer i64/u64: signed/unsigned 64-bit integer Constructors convert between integer widths: a = 42 b = i16(a) c = u32(b) A narrower destination may discard high bits rather than report an overflow. For example, u8(256) is 0. When a value comes from external input and must fit a particular format, checking its range before conversion makes that requirement explicit. The compiler's numerical-semantics flag does not turn fixed-width integers into arbitrary-precision values. Similarly, you can perform arithmetic operations on integers of the same types: x = i32(10) y = i32(20) print(x + y) # 30 The shift operators << and >> also accept a standard int (Int[64]) as the right-hand operand for any Int[N] or UInt[N]. In this case, the result keeps the left-hand operand's type rather than promoting the operands to a common integer type. For example, i8(3) << 2 has type i8 and value 12.

Codon's standard float type represents a 64-bit floating-point value (IEEE 754 binary64). Codon supports several alternative floating-point types: float32: 32-bit floating-point value (IEEE 754 binary32) float16: 16-bit floating-point value (IEEE 754 binary16) float128: 128-bit floating-point value (IEEE 754 binary128) bfloat16: a 16-bit floating-point value with 7 explicit fraction bits and 8 exponent bits. Its exponent range is comparable to float32, not the standard 64-bit float, and its reduced precision suits workloads where range matters more than fine-grained numerical accuracy. Each of these float types can be constructed from a standard float: x = float32(3.14) y = float128(-1.0) z = bfloat16(0.5) They all also support the usual arithmetic operators: x = bfloat16(2) ** bfloat16(0.5) print(x) # 1.41406

Codon supports raw pointers natively via the Ptr type, which is parameterized by the type of the object being pointed to (i.e. Ptr[int] is an int pointer, Ptr[float] is a float pointer, and so on). danger Pointer operations are not bounds-checked, meaning dereferencing an invalid pointer can cause a segmentation fault. Buffers of a specific type can be dynamically allocated by constructing a Ptr type with an integer argument, representing the number of elements of the given type to allocate: buffer = Ptr[int](10) This allocates storage for ten integers through Codon's garbage collector. Although the result behaves like a C pointer, it is not a malloc() allocation that the caller should pass to free(). Elements should be assigned before they are read. A pointer obtained from an external C library instead follows that library's allocation and release rules. Pointers can be dereferenced and indexed: buffer = Ptr[int](10) buffer[0] = 10 # equivalent to '(*buffer) = 10' in C buffer[5] = 42 # equivalent to 'buffer[5] = 42' in C print(buffer[0]) # 10 print(buffer[5]) # 42 Constructing a pointer without any arguments results in a null pointer: null = Ptr[int]() # equivalent to 'NULL' in C or 'nullptr' in C++ You can cast between different pointer types: x = Ptr[float](1) x[0] = 3.14 y = Ptr[int](x) # treat 'x' as an integer pointer print(y[0]) # 4614253070214989087 - same bits as '3.14' float Pointers support various arithmetic and comparison operators: p = Ptr[int](1) q = p + 1 # equivalent to '&p[1]' in C print(p == q) # False print(q - p) # 1 print(p < q) # True

It is possible to obtain a pointer to a variable via the __ptr__ intrinsic function: x = 42 p = __ptr__(x) # 'p' is a 'Ptr[int]'; equivalent to '&x' in C p[0] = 99 print(x) # 99 Pointers to variables can be useful when interfacing with C APIs. For example, consider the C standard library function frexp() which stores one of its outputs in an argument pointer. We can call this function from Codon as follows: from C import frexp(float, Ptr[i32]) -> float x = 16.4 exponent = i32() mantissa = frexp(x, __ptr__(exponent)) # equivalent to 'frexp(x, &exponent)' in C print(mantissa, exponent) # 0.5125 5 The pointer in this example is borrowed only for the duration of frexp(). A pointer to a local variable does not extend that variable's lifetime, so it should not be returned or retained by a C API that will use it after the function exits. An allocated buffer with an appropriate owner is needed for longer-lived storage. Refer to C/C++ integration for more information about calling C/C++ functions from Codon.

__ptr__ can also be used to obtain pointers to fields of tuple classes: @tuple class Point: x: int y: int r = Point(3, 4) p = __ptr__(r.y) # 'p' is a 'Ptr[int]'; equivalent to '&r.y' in C p[0] = 99 print(r.x, r.y) # 3 99 This is an unsafe, low-level operation that bypasses the normal restriction on assigning tuple fields. Tuple classes are passed by value, so modifying the storage of one local value does not modify a previously copied value: @tuple class Point: x: int y: int r = Point(3, 4) s = r # creates a copy of 'r' p = __ptr__(r.y) p[0] = 99 print(s.x, s.y) # 3 4 (not changed by pointer modification)

Pointers have several methods to facilitate software prefetching. These methods all have the form __prefetch_[rw][0123]__, where [rw] indicates whether the prefetch is made for a "read" (r) or a "write" (w), and the [0123] is a temporal locality specifier, with higher values indicating more locality (i.e. that the value should be kept in cache). For example: p = Ptr[int](1) p.__prefetch_w3__() # prefetch for write, high temporal locality Refer to LLVM's prefetch intrinsic for additional information. warning Not all targets support software prefetching. Consult the relevant documentation for your instruction set architecture for more information.

Arrays can be allocated on the stack via the __array__ intrinsic function: def f(): arr = __array__[int](10) # array of 10 integers; equivalent to 'int64_t arr[10]' in C arr[0] = 42 print(arr[0]) # 42 f() __array__[T](N) returns a Ptr[T] pointing to storage for N elements. The size must be a literal integer and is not stored in the pointer, so code that needs the length can keep it separately. The returned pointer can be indexed directly, as above, or passed to a function accepting Ptr[T]. The storage belongs to the current function invocation. As with a pointer to a local variable, arr must not escape to code that could use it after the function returns; a garbage-collected buffer is a better choice when the storage needs to outlive that call.

Codon supports compile-time metaprogramming through the special Literal type. Literals represent constants which can be operated on and manipulated at compile time. There are three types of Literals: Literal[int]: integer constant Literal[str]: string constant Literal[bool]: boolean constant

Integer literals can be defined explicitly as follows: n: Literal[int] = 42 Literals must be known at compile time. For example, the following code will cause a compilation error: from sys import argv n: Literal[int] = len(argv) # error: value is not literal! Arithmetic operations on integer literals result in other integer literals: n: Literal[int] = 42 m: Literal[int] = n + 1 # valid int literal Conditional expressions on literals also result in other literals: n: Literal[int] = 42 m: Literal[int] = n//2 if n%2 == 0 else 3*n + 1 Integer literals can be passed as function arguments, and also returned from functions: def fib(n: Literal[int]) -> Literal[int]: return 1 if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) n: Literal[int] = fib(10) # computed entirely at compile time!

Much like integer literals, string literals represent constant strings: s: Literal[str] = 'hello' Whereas integer literals can be manipulated via arithmetic operations to produce other integer literals, string literals can be manipulated via string operations to produce new string literals: t: Literal[str] = s[1] # 'e' u: Literal[str] = s[3:] # 'lo' Much like integer literals, string literals can similarly be used in literal conditional expressions and as function argument or return types.

Finally, boolean literals represent constant booleans: b: Literal[bool] = True Boolean operators can be used on boolean literals to produce new boolean literals: b: Literal[bool] = True d: Literal[bool] = not b # False Some operations on integer and string literals produce boolean literals: n: Literal[int] = 42 s: Literal[str] = 'hello' b: Literal[bool] = (n < 10) # False d: Literal[bool] = (s[2:4] == 'll') # True

It is also possible to express loops where the loop index is a literal integer, via the codon.static module: import codon.static for i in static.range(10): m: Literal[int] = 3*i + 1 print(m) Static loops are unrolled at compile time, which allows the loop index to take on literal values. Static loops can also be used to create tuples, the lengths of which must be compile-time constants in Codon: import codon.static t = tuple(i*i for i in static.range(5)) print(t) # (0, 1, 4, 9, 16) You can loop over another tuple by obtaining its length as an integer literal via static.len(): import codon.static t = tuple(i*i for i in static.range(5)) u = tuple(t[i] + 1 for i in static.range(static.len(t))) print(u) # (1, 2, 5, 10, 17)

Literal expressions can be used as conditions in if statements, which enables the compiler to eliminate branches that it knows will not be entered at runtime. This can be used to avoid type checking errors, for example: def foo(x): if isinstance(x, int): return x + 1 elif isinstance(x, str): return x + '!' else: return x print(foo(42)) # 43 print(foo('hello')) # hello! print(foo(3.14)) # 3.14 Normally, Codon's type checker would flag an expression like x + 1 as an error if the type of x is str. However, in the code above, the branches that are not applicable to the type of x are eliminated so as to allow the code to type check and compile. Here is another, more involved example: def flatten(x): if isinstance(x, list): for a in x: flatten(a) else: print(x) flatten([[1,2,3], [], [4, 5], [6]]) # 1, 2, ..., 6 Standard static typing on this program would be problematic since, if x is an int, it would not be iterable and hence would produce an error on for a in x. Static evaluation solves this problem by evaluating isinstance(x, list) at compile time and avoiding type checking the block containing the loop when x is not a list. Static evaluation works with literal expressions and with checks such as isinstance(), hasattr() and type comparisons when their results are known during compilation. In the examples above, each function specialization has a concrete input type, so only the applicable branch needs to be compiled. An isinstance() check is not necessarily a compile-time operation: a union value or a base-typed object can require a runtime check to determine which alternative is present. The syntax is the same, but the available type information determines when the decision can be made.

Markdown Codon uses Python's syntax and familiar programming constructs, including functions, classes, comprehensions, generators and exceptions. The main difference is how a program runs: Codon determines native types before execution and compiles operations on those types to machine code, rather than evaluating them through the CPython interpreter. Type annotations are often optional because the compiler can infer types from assignments and function calls. For example, the same unannotated function can be compiled for integer and floating-point inputs: def squared_total(values): return sum(value * value for value in values) print(squared_total([1, 2, 3])) # 14 print(squared_total([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])) # 14.0 Both calls use the same source definition, but operate on different native element types. The generics guide explains this specialization model in more detail, including how to describe types explicitly when an API needs a particular representation. The rest of this section covers functions and generators, classes, exceptions and resources, compile-time metaprogramming and low-level facilities. Python libraries can also be used through Python interoperability, which is particularly useful when a dependency relies on dynamic Python behavior.

tip Found something that works differently in Codon than Python which isn't mentioned below? Let us know on GitHub. Python source often needs little adaptation, but its data representations and runtime assumptions still matter. The differences below are useful to consider when moving an existing program to Codon, especially at file formats, numerical boundaries and calls into other libraries.

Integers: Codon's int is a 64-bit signed integer, whereas Python's integers can grow to arbitrary precision. Int[N] and UInt[N] provide other fixed widths; choosing a larger N changes the available range, but does not make an integer grow automatically. See low-level types for their use and C equivalents. Tuples: Ordinary tuples have a fixed number of fields whose types are known at compile time. Python-style tuple(iterable) conversion is not generally supported; a list is a more suitable representation when a sequence's length is determined at runtime. Arrays: Codon includes a native NumPy implementation with a corresponding ndarray type. Codon's ndarray is parameterized by the data type (dtype) and dimension (ndim). In practice, this almost never affects NumPy code as these parameters are determined automatically at compile time. In some cases, such as when reading array data from disk, they must be provided programmatically. Learn more in the Codon-NumPy docs.

Codon needs to determine the type of each expression before execution. A function can be generic, as in the example above, but each compiled specialization still has known argument and return types. An annotation can help express an interface or resolve an otherwise ambiguous empty collection: counts: dict[str, int] = {} for name in ["oak", "pine", "oak"]: counts[name] = counts.get(name, 0) + 1 print(counts["oak"]) # 2 Runtime changes to a class's fields or methods do not fit this compilation model. When an application requires that kind of dynamism, the affected code can remain in Python and be called through the interoperability layer. For native code, generic types and compile-time specialization offer ways to share implementations without changing their layout at runtime.

Python-style numerical semantics are the default. For example, integer floor division rounds down, and division by zero raises an exception. Programs that can work with C-style behavior may opt into -numerics=c, which changes operations such as signed division and some numerical error checks in exchange for additional optimization opportunities. This choice is independent of -debug and -release; enabling optimization does not by itself select C-style numerics. Neither numerical mode changes the fixed width of int. The usage guide shows examples of the differences.
While most of the commonly used builtin modules have Codon-native implementations, a few are not yet implemented. However these can still be used within Codon via from python import.

Command-line parsing with a tagged ArgumentValue and a dynamic Namespace. Parsed attributes are tagged values: use args.count.as_int(), args.name.as_str(), and args.files.values() to access native values.

Named action registration normalizes constructor arguments to the standard Action fields and does not forward additional constructor keywords. Pass the action class directly to supply custom keywords.

Positional arguments: Custom actions are supported only for options. Using a custom class, factory, or registered action for a positional raises TypeError before construction. Initializer overloads: Class construction checks only the leading __init__ signature exposed by the compiler; it does not search additional overloads or base initializers. Use a single initializer, or a factory that explicitly calls the desired overload. Parser defaults: For direct classes and factories, defaults from set_defaults() and argument_default are passed as ArgumentValue, not unboxed to a native constructor parameter type. Leave the default parameter unannotated or accept ArgumentValue; alternatively, pass default= directly to add_argument(), which preserves its native type. Incompatible signatures are rejected at compile time when independent of parser defaults, and with TypeError when they depend on runtime parser defaults.

Native JSON parsing and encoding with a tagged JSON value. Provides load, loads, dump, dumps, JSONDecoder, JSONEncoder, and JSONDecodeError. Standard formatting options and non-finite number defaults follow Python. import json value = json.loads('{"items": [1, true, null]}') number = value["items"][0].as_int() value["items"].append("text") print(json.dumps(value, indent=2)) Differences from Python: Decoding returns JSON. Use kind, is_null(), and typed accessors as_bool(), as_int(), as_float(), as_str(); wrong kinds raise TypeError (as_float() also accepts integers). JSON() is null; JSON(value) converts supported native scalars, optionals, lists, tuples, and string-keyed dicts. JSON.array() and JSON.object() create empty containers. Use values(), keys(), or items() instead of direct iteration. Containers support indexing and mutation; copies share storage. Scalars are immutable. Equality is structural and kind-sensitive (JSON(1) != JSON(1.0)); values are unhashable. str(value) serializes JSON, including quotes around strings. Integers are signed 64-bit; oversized literals raise OverflowError. Fractional and exponent-form numbers use binary64. Keys must be strings. skipkeys, cls, default, object_hook, object_pairs_hook, parse_int, parse_float, and parse_constant are unsupported; unsupported native types, including nested members, are compile-time errors. Parsing/encoding use max_depth=512, raising RecursionError when exceeded, even with check_circular=False. Structural comparison also has a 512 limit. I/O is not streaming: load() reads the whole stream; dump() writes a complete string to a text stream. iterencode() is not provided. Decode-error locations use Unicode code points; trailing-comma diagnostics follow CPython 3.14. class JSON @tuple class JSON View complete class API → Two-word value with a packed tag and string metadata, plus scalar bits or a pointer. Windows backend for os; native little-endian Windows x64/ARM64 only. All foreign declarations are local to functions and nothing calls Windows at module initialization. The public os module supplies compile-time dispatch and the environ mapping. This module does not import os or port the compiler/runtime. Called functions require Kernel32 and a compatible Microsoft UCRT; no new C++ runtime helpers are needed. Paths, commands and environment use UTF-16LE with surrogatepass, never ANSI. getcwdb() uses UTF-8 with surrogatepass, as modern Python on Windows does. Extended-length paths are accepted as supplied; no automatic long-path prefix/manifest is added. mkdir() ignores mode and inherits the parent's Windows security descriptor (even for 0o700); chmod() changes only the read-only attribute. access() is an attribute probe, not an ACL check, and X_OK means existence. Descriptor I/O retains the descriptor's CRT text/binary mode and can return partial transfers. Environment updates are not atomic across the CRT and OS and must be externally synchronized with other environment writers. The CRT treats an empty value as deletion; putenv() restores an actual empty OS value afterwards, but cannot make CRT getenv() distinguish empty from missing. Other CRT instances/ANSI mirrors cannot be kept fully Unicode-consistent. No snapshot is updated here. OSError carries errno, strerror, applicable filenames and the original winerror for Windows API failures. CRT failures supply errno without inventing winerror. Toolhelp reports the recorded parent PID, which can have exited or been reused. Descriptive statistics and distributions for native numeric data. The API follows CPython 3.14, including weighted means, ranked correlation, regression, and kernel density estimation. Numeric aggregates return float; median_low, median_high, and modes preserve the input element type. Compensated floating-point arithmetic and widened integer intermediates avoid common cancellation and overflow errors, but do not provide Decimal/Fraction arithmetic. Random sampling accepts integer seeds. Remove NaNs before computing order statistics; native floats do not retain Python object identity for NaNs. Finite product overflow uses a fixed-point recovery accumulator.
